Tomato_Late_blight.disease_cycle: Infected material -> initial lesion -> spore production on wet leaves -> airborne or splash spread -> repeated infection cycles -> fruit and canopy collapse under favorable weather.
how_it_spreads: Spores move by wind and weather-driven spread.
Rain splash can help spread inoculum locally.
Wet weather increases secondary infection rates.
Tomato_Late_blight.environmental_risk: A few days of cool wet weather can be enough to trigger rapid epidemic spread once lesions are established.
early_symptoms: Lesions expanding quickly under cool wet weather

symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The oomycete infects and kills tissue rapidly when leaf surfaces stay wet and cool.
symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This appears in cool wet weather and after the first infection cycle is established.

leaf_symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This happens during favorable weather and active secondary cycles.
leaf_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The disease is severe and canopy function is rapidly declining.

stem_symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This occurs later, often in heavily infected canopies.
stem_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The disease is not limited to leaf tissue and the plant is under severe stress.

fruit_symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: Fruit tissues are invaded and lose integrity when the disease is active.
fruit_symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This occurs during severe wet conditions and epidemic progression.
fruit_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: Fruit can be lost to disease or secondary decay.

root_or_tuber_symptoms: Not a primary symptom in tomato late blight, though fruit quality losses are important.
Tomato_Late_blight.disease_progression: Once the epidemic begins, the disease can intensify quickly as conditions remain cool and wet, which may lead to major canopy loss and fruit infection.

monitoring: Scout frequently during cool wet weather

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.definition: A foliar fungal disease of tomato favored by high humidity and dense plant canopies, especially in protected cultivation.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.detailed_description: Leaf mold develops when relative humidity remains high and leaf surfaces stay wet for prolonged periods. It is commonly associated with dense canopies and poor ventilation in greenhouses or tunnels.

disease_triangle.pathogen: Passalora fulva infects tomato foliage when humidity stays high and the pathogen can reproduce on leaf tissue.
disease_triangle.host: Tomato plants with dense canopy structure and poor airflow are highly susceptible.
disease_triangle.environment: High humidity and poor ventilation create the most favorable conditions for infection and spread.

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.why_it_occurs: The fungus reproduces well when relative humidity stays high and the foliage remains moist, leading to repeated infections and a large number of spores on the lower leaf surface.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.how_it_starts: Infection usually starts on older lower leaves beneath a dense canopy and can continue upward when conditions remain humid.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.disease_cycle: Leaf infection -> sporulation on lower leaf surfaces -> spore release -> infection of adjacent leaf surfaces under high humidity -> repeated cycles in dense canopies.
how_it_spreads: Spores disperse through air movement within the canopy.
High humidity supports repeated sporulation.
Dense canopies maintain favorable conditions.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.environmental_risk: High humidity and reduced airflow keep surfaces wet and allow the fungus to repeat its infection cycle across the canopy.
early_symptoms: Pale yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces

symptom_explanations.symptom: Pale yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces
symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The fungus infects the tissue and the host responds with a visible yellowing around lesions.
symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: Symptoms appear as the disease develops in humid or poorly ventilated conditions.
symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The disease is active and the canopy environment is strongly favoring pathogen reproduction.

leaf_symptoms: Leaves may wither and stay attached

leaf_symptom_explanations.symptom: Velvety olive growth on leaf undersides
leaf_symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The pathogen forms spore-bearing structures on the lower leaf surface under favorable humidity.
leaf_symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This occurs after infection is established and high humidity persists.
leaf_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The disease is reproducing and can spread to neighboring tissues.

fruit_symptoms: Some fruit lesions can occur in severe infections.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.disease_progression: The disease usually moves from lower leaves upward as humidity remains high and infected tissue continues to produce spores.

Avoid dense canopies and rapid wetness accumulation

Follow local extension recommendations for disease management

Dense wet foliage

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.important_note: Leaf mold is particularly important in protected cultivation and can spread rapidly when humidity is excessive.

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.definition: A common tomato foliar disease that usually begins on lower leaves and can lead to progressive defoliation under warm, wet conditions.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.detailed_description: Septoria leaf spot is especially common on lower leaves after fruit set. It is favored by wet leaves, warm weather and a dense canopy, and repeated infection cycles can cause widespread defoliation.

disease_triangle.pathogen: The fungus survives on infected residue and produces spores when conditions remain favorable.
disease_triangle.host: Tomato foliage, especially older lower leaves, is susceptible.
disease_triangle.environment: Warm temperatures, humidity and prolonged leaf wetness allow repeated infection cycles.

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.why_it_occurs: The fungus produces many spores on infected tissue, and repeated wet periods allow it to move into new foliage quickly.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.how_it_starts: Lower leaves are commonly infected first, and disease then progresses upward when weather remains moist and the canopy remains dense.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.disease_cycle: Infected debris -> spore release -> lower leaf infection -> lesions with fruiting bodies -> repeated spore cycles -> defoliation and canopy decline.
how_it_spreads: Water splashing disperses spores.
Wind can carry spores short distances.
Infected residue increases risk in subsequent crops.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.environmental_risk: Warm wet periods enable repeated cycles of infection and lead to defoliation when the disease persists.
early_symptoms: Small dark spots on lower leaves
Tyical tan-gray centers with darker margins

symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The fungus kills tissue in the lesion center while the surrounding tissue remains active.
symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: Lesions become fully visible as the disease matures under warm wet weather.
symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The crop is experiencing active fungal infection and defoliation may follow.

leaf_symptom_explanations.symptom: Small spots with tan centers and dark fruiting bodies
leaf_symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The fungus forms fruiting structures in the tissue as it progresses through its reproduction stage.
leaf_symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This occurs as the lesion matures under repeated wet periods.
leaf_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The plant is in an active infection cycle and new spores are being produced.

stem_symptoms: Occasional petiole or stem involvement can occur under severe disease pressure.
fruit_symptoms: Not a major symptom; fruit is typically not the primary site of infection.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.disease_progression: Usually progresses from lower leaves upward, causing yellowing, leaf death and a decline in overall plant vigor as photosynthetic tissue is lost.

Warm wet weather and sequential canopy spread

Check for lesion pattern and defoliation

Remove lower infected foliage when appropriate

Ignoring lower-leaf lesions
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.when_to_seek_expert_help: Seek expert guidance if defoliation is severe, the diagnosis is uncertain or control strategies are not working.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.important_note: The disease can lead to significant defoliation, raising the risk of fruit sunscald and reduced yield.

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.definition: A mite pest that feeds on plant cells, causing stippling, bronzing and reduced vigor under hot dry conditions.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.detailed_description: Spider mites thrive under hot, dry and dusty conditions and often feed on the undersides of leaves. Infestations can build rapidly and become serious if plant stress remains high.

disease_triangle.pathogen: The pest reproduces quickly under hot, dry weather and high plant stress.
disease_triangle.host: Tomato plants under water stress or in hot dry conditions are particularly vulnerable.
disease_triangle.environment: Hot, dry, dusty weather and reduced humidity favor pest population growth.

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.why_it_occurs: Mites feed on cells and rapidly build populations when weather is dry and plants are physiologically stressed.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.how_it_starts: Infestations often begin on leaf undersides and spread as the colony increases under hot, dry conditions.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.disease_cycle: Initial feeding -> rapid population increase -> more stippling and webbing -> leaf bronzing -> defoliation under severe stress.
how_it_spreads: Wind moves mites between plants.
Movement along plant surfaces supports spread.
Hot dry weather favors population growth.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.environmental_risk: Hot dry weather drives rapid mite multiplication and severe feeding damage, which can reduce photosynthesis and plant vigor quickly.

symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: Mites pierce plant cells and remove chlorophyll-rich contents, causing visible pale spotting.
symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This appears under hot dry conditions and on older leaves before a severe outbreak.
symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The plants are being fed on and mite pressure is increasing.

leaf_symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: Repeated feeding reduces leaf function, causing chlorophyll loss and premature senescence.
leaf_symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This usually develops after mite populations have increased substantially.
leaf_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The plant is under intense feeding pressure and is losing photosynthetic area.

fruit_symptoms: Not a major symptom for this pest.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.disease_progression: Leaf damage worsens as mite numbers increase, reducing photosynthesis and increasing plant stress, with severe outbreaks causing bronzing and leaf drop.

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.important_note: This is a pest issue rather than a plant pathogen disease; the symptoms are caused by mite feeding.

Tomato__Target_Spot.definition: A fungal tomato disease that can affect leaves, petioles, stems and fruit, especially in warm humid crops with dense canopies.
Tomato__Target_Spot.detailed_description: Target spot is favored by warm, wet conditions and prolonged canopy moisture. It is notable because the symptoms can resemble early blight or bacterial spot, especially when the disease is not yet well differentiated.

disease_triangle.pathogen: The fungus can survive and spread in moist canopies and infected debris.
disease_triangle.host: Susceptible tomato foliage and fruit are most vulnerable.
disease_triangle.environment: Warm temperatures, humidity and prolonged leaf wetness support disease development.

Tomato__Target_Spot.why_it_occurs: The pathogen moves efficiently under warm wet canopy conditions, causing repeated lesions and tissue collapse when infection pressure remains high.
Tomato__Target_Spot.how_it_starts: Disease often begins on older leaves or within dense canopy zones and then spreads as spores are produced on infected tissue.
Tomato__Target_Spot.disease_cycle: Initial infection -> lesion development -> sporulation -> spread within canopy -> repeated cycles under wet warm conditions.
how_it_spreads: Wind and rainfall move spores.
Dense canopies retain moisture and increase spread.
Infected tissues contribute inoculum for secondary cycles.
Tomato__Target_Spot.environmental_risk: The disease becomes more dangerous when warm wet periods persist because repeated spore cycles help lesions expand and merge.

symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The pathogen creates a radial lesion pattern as tissue is repeatedly invaded and damaged.
symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This occurs under warm humid conditions and with persistent leaf wetness.
symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: Disease is active and may be spreading within the crop canopy.

leaf_symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The pathogen damages more tissue over time and the surrounding plant tissues respond with chlorosis.
leaf_symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This happens as the disease progresses under humid warm weather.
leaf_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The disease is substantially reducing the leaf function of the plant.

stem_symptoms: Dark oval lesions may appear on stems.
fruit_symptoms: Small brown sunken lesions may form on fruit
Fruit may develop pitting or cracking
Tomato__Target_Spot.disease_progression: Target spot typically intensifies in warm humid canopies and can eventually reduce leaf function, fruit quality and overall yield.
identification: Potential fruit lesions and stem involvement
monitoring: Inspect lower and middle canopy foliage
Check fruit and stems for lesions
Monitor humidity and canopy density
management: Remove infected plant material where appropriate
Follow local extension advice for disease management
what_to_avoid: Ignoring lesion overlap with early blight or bacterial spot
Leaving dense infected canopy in place
Persistent wet foliage
Tomato__Target_Spot.when_to_seek_expert_help: Seek local plant pathology advice when the diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms continue despite sanitation and canopy management.
Tomato__Target_Spot.important_note: Symptoms can overlap with other tomato leaf-spot diseases, so careful comparison and local guidance are important.

Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.scientific_name: Begomovirus; tomato yellow leaf curl virus
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.definition: A viral disease transmitted by whiteflies that causes leaf curling, yellowing, stunting and reduced reproductive development in tomato.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.detailed_description: TYLCV is spread by whiteflies and can severely reduce plant vigor and fruit yield when infected transplants are introduced or when vector populations are not managed. The disease is not caused by a fungal leaf-spot organism.

disease_triangle.pathogen: The virus is transmitted by whiteflies and may persist in infected plants.
disease_triangle.host: Susceptible tomato cultivars are highly affected.
disease_triangle.environment: Whitefly populations and infected transplants create the strongest risk for disease establishment.

Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.why_it_occurs: The virus is introduced by whitefly vectors and then spreads within the crop, leading to poor leaf function and stunting.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.how_it_starts: Infection often begins after whiteflies feed on a healthy plant, or when infected transplants are introduced into a field.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.disease_cycle: Vector feeding -> virus acquisition -> transmission to healthy plants -> symptom development -> reduced growth and fruit production -> ongoing spread in presence of vectors.
how_it_spreads: Whiteflies carry and spread the virus.
Infected transplants can introduce it.
Nearby infected volunteer hosts can maintain pressure.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.environmental_risk: Warm weather can favor whitefly populations and increase transmission, which raises the chance of widespread infection.

symptom_explanations.symptom: Upward leaf curling and small leaves
symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The virus interferes with normal plant growth and development, causing distorted leaf architecture and stunting.
symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: Symptoms appear after vector feeding and virus establishment.
symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The plant is infected with a systemic virus and growth is being compromised.

leaf_symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The virus disrupts normal chlorophyll production and leaf growth regulation.
leaf_symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: This appears after the virus establishes in the plant.
leaf_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The plant is systemically infected and photosynthesis may be reduced.

fruit_symptoms: Reduced fruit set and smaller fruit due to plant stress.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.disease_progression: The plant often becomes progressively stunted as the virus impairs normal growth and fruit set, especially when whiteflies remain active.

monitoring: Monitor whiteflies
Inspect new growth for yellowing and curling
Check transplants before planting
cultural_prevention: Prompt removal of severely diseased plants
management: Follow local extension recommendations for vector management

Introducing suspicious transplants
Leaving severely diseased plants in place
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.when_to_seek_expert_help: Seek local agricultural or extension advice when symptoms are widespread, when whitefly pressure is high, or when cultivar choice and vector management are uncertain.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.important_note: TYLCV is a virus disease, not a fungal leaf-spot disease, and whitefly management is central to control.

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.causal_agent: Tomato mosaic virus and related tobamoviruses
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.definition: A viral disease that produces mottling, leaf deformation and sometimes fruit abnormalities, often spread by contaminated handling or infected seed and seedlings.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.detailed_description: Tomato mosaic virus can spread mechanically, which means workers, tools and plants can move the virus without insect vectors. The disease is stable and can persist on surfaces and in infected residues.

disease_triangle.pathogen: The virus persists on surfaces and in infected plant material and spreads by mechanical contact.
disease_triangle.host: Tomato plants are susceptible and the virus can establish quickly in newly infected tissue.
disease_triangle.environment: Human handling and contaminated equipment strongly influence spread, rather than purely weather conditions.

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.why_it_occurs: The virus is spread through contact and contaminated tools, so any handling that moves sap from infected plants to healthy tissues can cause new infections.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.how_it_starts: Initially infected plants or contaminated tools can transfer sap to healthy leaves, allowing the virus to establish.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.disease_cycle: Virus introduction -> infection of healthy tissues -> systemic spread in plant -> mosaic symptoms and possible fruit abnormalities -> continued spread through contaminated handling.
how_it_spreads: Mechanical contact with infected plants.
Contaminated hands, tools and equipment.
Infected seedling or propagative material.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.environmental_risk: This disease is less about weather and more about contamination and crop handling; the biggest risk is movement of sap between plants or tools.
early_symptoms: Mottled light and dark green foliage

symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The virus interferes with normal chlorophyll production and tissue formation.
symptom_explanations.when_it_occurs: Symptoms appear after infection is established and the virus is systemic.
symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The plant is infected and development is being disrupted.

leaf_symptoms: Fern-like or malformed leaves in severe cases

leaf_symptom_explanations.why_it_occurs: The virus disrupts normal cell development and pigment distribution, creating abnormal leaf shapes and color patterns.
leaf_symptom_explanations.what_it_indicates: The plant is affected by a systemic viral disorder.

fruit_symptoms: Fruit may show abnormal patterns or reduced quality in some infections.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.disease_progression: Symptoms can remain on foliage and fruit over time, and the disease continues to affect plant vigor when the infected tissue is retained in the crop.

monitoring: Inspect new growth and leaf color patterns
Review sanitation and handling practices
Check transplants before planting

cultural_prevention: Avoid washing healthy plants after handling infected ones without sanitation
Plan crop operations to reduce spread
management: Remove severely diseased plants according to local guidance
Follow local extension recommendations for disease management
what_to_avoid: Handling healthy plants after infected ones without cleaning
Reusing contaminated tools
Ignoring mosaic symptoms
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.when_to_seek_expert_help: Seek local agricultural advice when virus identification is uncertain, when the crop is heavily affected, or when management decisions depend on distinguishing virus symptoms from other disorders.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.important_note: This is a virus disease spread primarily by sap movement and contaminated handling rather than by weather alone.
